skills.name: Match statistical questions to the displays that answer them
skills.i_do_script: Every data display was built to answer some statistical question -- and every display throws information away. I'll project a line plot of quiz scores and ask: could this answer 'How many students scored 8?' Yes -- count dots. Could it answer 'Which STUDENT scored 8?' Never -- the names are gone; dots don't wear name tags. The routine I model: read the axis labels to reconstruct what was measured, then check whether the question asks for something the display kept or something it threw away.

canonical_error.pattern: Matches a question to a display that cannot answer it -- usually a question about a named individual, exact values a grouped display discarded, or data that was never collected
canonical_error.example: Shown a box plot of mile-run times, picks 'Which student ran the fastest mile?' as the question it answers, because 'fastest' seems visible at the whisker's end.
canonical_error.why: The student treats a display as a window onto everything about the situation. They haven't internalized that a display only keeps certain features of the data set -- and identities, exact grouped values, and uncollected facts are not among them.

redirect_script.stop: Check -- did the display keep that information?
redirect_script.prompt: Read the axis labels out loud: what was measured, and about whom? Now ask -- does the question want something you can point to in the display, or something the display threw away, like names or exact values?
redirect_script.praise: You tested the question against what the display actually keeps -- perfect match.

vocabulary.definition: A picture of a data set -- like a line plot, histogram, or box plot.
A bar graph that counts how many data values fall in each interval; bars touch because the intervals connect.
A five-number picture of a data set showing minimum, quartiles, median, and maximum -- the spread, not individual values.
A range of values grouped together, like 60-119 minutes.
The whole collection of values a display represents.

worked_example_script.text: Project the line plot of class quiz scores (dots stacked over 6 through 10).
Before anything else -- read the axis label. What was measured, and about whom? So what question do you think the teacher asked?
The axis says 'Quiz score' and each dot is a student -- the teacher asked something like 'What score did each student get?'
Candidate question 1: 'How many students scored 8?' Can this plot answer it? Point to where.
Candidate question 2: 'WHICH student scored 10?' Look hard at that dot above 10. Can you tell me who it is?
This is the trap. If the student starts guessing names, stop: the dot has no name tag. Displays keep values and counts -- identities are thrown away.
Candidate question 3: 'How long did each student study?' Is study time anywhere in this display?
No -- that data was never collected. So the test is: reconstruct what was measured from the labels, then only match questions asking for what the display kept.
Your turn: write one question this plot CAN answer and one it CANNOT, and say why.

practice_problems.stem: A line plot shows one dot per student above their number of pets. Can it answer 'How many students have 3 pets?' Why?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- count the dots above 3; the plot keeps every value and its frequency.

practice_problems.stem: Name one thing a box plot does NOT show about a data set.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: individual data values (or exact frequencies, or how many data points there are).

practice_problems.stem: A histogram of daily step counts uses intervals of 2,000 steps. Can it answer 'Exactly how many steps did the most active person take?' Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No -- the histogram only shows that the top value falls somewhere inside the last interval, not its exact value.
practice_problems.notes: Displays-lose-information reasoning.

practice_problems.stem: A frequency table shows 'Hours of sleep' intervals with student counts. Write one statistical question this table CAN answer.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 'How many students slept between 7 and 8 hours?' or 'How many hours of sleep did students in the class get?'
practice_problems.notes: Producing a matching question, not just picking one.

practice_problems.stem: Data collected: 'What is your favorite school subject?' A student wants a line plot. What's the problem, and what display works?
practice_problems.answer: Favorite subject is category data, not numbers on a line -- a line plot needs numeric values. A frequency table (or bar-style chart) of subjects fits.
practice_problems.notes: Matching display to data TYPE.

practice_problems.stem: A box plot summarizes 25 students' mile-run times. Find the flaw in Kenji's claim and fix it.
shown_work: Kenji looked at the box plot and said:
"This graph can tell me exactly which student ran a 9-minute mile,
because 9 is right there on the number line."
practice_problems.answer: The box plot's number line shows possible TIMES, not students -- names never appear in the display, and a box plot doesn't even show individual data values. It can answer questions about the whole data set, like 'What is the spread of mile times?', not questions about one identified person.
practice_problems.notes: Overreach error: asking a display for information it discarded.

practice_problems.stem: Write one statistical question a line plot of the same data could answer that a box plot could NOT, and one question both could answer.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: line-plot-only -- 'How many students scored exactly 8?' (box plots hide frequencies). Both -- 'What is the highest score in the data set?'
practice_problems.notes: Direct display-vs-display comparison; the heart of choosing a representation.

practice_problems.stem: A team asks: 'How many minutes does each sixth grader spend on the bus?' They collect 120 answers ranging from 2 to 95 minutes. Would you display it as a line plot or a histogram? Defend your choice.
practice_problems.answer: Histogram -- with 120 values spread over a wide range, a line plot would need ~94 tick marks and scattered dots; grouping into intervals (e.g., 0-14, 15-29...) shows the shape clearly.
practice_problems.notes: Design decision with a real trade-off; either answer accepted with sound reasoning about size/range.

activities.title: Question-to-Display Speed Match
materials: Card set: statistical questions and display descriptions
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs match each statistical question to the display that can answer it.
2. Rule: before matching, say what the display KEEPS (exact values? frequencies? spread?) and what it THROWS AWAY.
3. Decoy cards ask for information no display keeps (student names, future data) -- they get parked in a 'no display can answer this' zone.
4. Debrief: what did every parked card have in common?

How many movies run between 95 and 110 minutes?
pairs.right: Histogram of movie lengths in 15-minute intervals

pairs.left: How spread out are the plant heights from shortest to tallest?

pairs.right: Frequency table of reading minutes in intervals

decoys: Which student is the fastest runner?

activities.title: Can This Display Answer It?
materials: One projected line plot of 'minutes to get to school'
activities.instructions:
1. Project one line plot. Groups sort question cards into CAN ANSWER and CANNOT ANSWER.
2. Every CAN card must come with the answer; every CANNOT card must come with the reason (names lost? data not collected? exact values grouped away?).
3. Groups write one new question for each pile.
4. Debrief: displays answer questions about the DATA SET, never about identified individuals or data that wasn't collected.

cards.text: How many students take exactly 15 minutes?
What is the longest travel time in the class?
How many students were surveyed?
How many students take less than 10 minutes?
Which student lives farthest away?

Will travel times be longer next year?

activities.title: Display Designers
materials: Class data set from a previous survey
activities.instructions:
1. Each group receives the same class data set and a target question (one group: 'How often does each value occur?'; another: 'What's the overall spread?'; another: 'How many values in each interval?').
2. Groups choose and draw the display that best answers THEIR question (line plot, box plot outline, or grouped frequency table/histogram).
3. Gallery walk: other groups guess which question each display was built for.
4. Debrief: same data, different displays -- the question decides the display.

strategy_links.why: Deciding whether a display can answer a question is an argument -- pairs must voice the keep/throw-away reasoning before committing.
Kenji's box-plot overreach is a precise, discussable error that teaches what each display discards.
Thinking aloud while reading axis labels models how to reconstruct the original statistical question from a display.

questioning_prompts: What information does this display keep, and what did it throw away?
Does this question ask about the whole data set, or about one named person?
Could you answer this question just by looking at the display -- show me where?
The data was collected by asking what question? How do the axis labels tell you?
Why would a histogram be a poor choice for answering 'how many students scored exactly 8'?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student matches a display to a question about a named individual ('Which student...?') or asks a display for exact values it grouped away.
misconception_redirects.say: Point to where a student's name appears in this display. It's not there -- displays keep values, not identities. Ask instead: is the question about the whole data set? Then find where the display shows it.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked what the display actually keeps before matching -- that's the whole skill.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks the matching question by keyword overlap (the display says 'minutes' so any 'minutes' question matches).
misconception_redirects.say: Two questions can share every keyword and still need different data. Read the axis labels: what was measured, about whom, in what units? The matching question asks for exactly that.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched on what was measured, not on the words that happened to repeat.

quick_checks.prompt: Show a line plot: give me one question it CAN answer and one it CANNOT.
quick_checks.look_for: CAN = frequency/value/total questions; CANNOT = identity or uncollected-data questions. A 'cannot' like 'how many at 5?' means the student doesn't yet know what the plot keeps.

quick_checks.prompt: The axis of a display reads 'Number of pets.' What question was the class asked?
quick_checks.look_for: 'How many pets do you have?' Reconstructing the question from the axis label is the pass; reading off a frequency instead is a miss.

worked_solution.stem: A frequency table shows 'Minutes read per week' in intervals with a count of students for each interval. Which question did the teacher most likely ask: 'How many students in the class read?', 'How many books do you read per week?', or 'How many minutes per week do you read?'
worked_solution.answer: How many minutes per week do you read?

steps.math: Read the labels: 'Minutes read per week' + student counts
steps.annotation: The axis and header tell you exactly what was measured (minutes of reading) and about whom (students).

steps.math: Eliminate: 'How many students read?' -> one number, not a table
steps.annotation: That question has a single answer; it couldn't fill a table of intervals with different counts.
Books would make the intervals counts of books, not minutes. The remaining question -- minutes per week -- matches the data exactly.

faded_example.stem: A histogram shows 'Daily step count' in intervals of 2,000 with bars counting days. Which question can it answer: 'Exactly how many steps were taken on the busiest day?' or 'How many days had between 6,000 and 8,000 steps?'
faded_example.answer: How many days had between 6,000 and 8,000 steps? (histograms keep interval counts, not exact values)

skills.name: Analyze data displays to draw and defend conclusions
skills.i_do_script: The top of this standard is using a display to answer the original statistical question with a defended conclusion. I'll model with a histogram of 18 tree heights (bars 2, 5, 8, 3): first anchor both axes out loud -- sideways is FEET, up is NUMBER OF TREES -- then build a claim with evidence: 'Most trees are 12 to 16 feet, because those bars hold 5 + 8 = 13 of the 18 trees.' Every conclusion gets a 'because' with counts in it. And I name the trap: the tallest bar reaching 8 does NOT mean any tree is 8 feet tall.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads the frequency (bar height or stack size) as if it were a data value, or asserts conclusions the display cannot support
canonical_error.example: Looking at a tree-height histogram whose tallest bar reaches 8 over the 14-16 ft interval, concludes 'the tallest tree is 8 feet' -- or claims 'a tree is exactly 15 feet tall' when exact values were grouped away.
canonical_error.why: The student hasn't anchored the two axes as different kinds of numbers: the horizontal axis carries the measured values, the vertical axis counts how many. Under analysis pressure the two collapse into one, and conclusions detach from the counts that must support them.

redirect_script.stop: Freeze -- which axis does that number live on?
redirect_script.prompt: Touch the bottom axis and say what it measures; touch the side axis and say what it counts. Then restate your conclusion as: 'Most of the data is between ___ and ___ because those bars hold ___ out of ___ values.'
redirect_script.praise: Interval plus counts plus a because -- that conclusion would hold up anywhere.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Evaluating a claim forces adding the correct bars. Students who eyeball 'the bars on the left exist, so yes' skip the counts.

sample_items.stem: The box plots show how many minutes students in two classes spent reviewing for a quiz. Write one comparison conclusion the plots support.
sample_items.answer: Sample: Class B generally reviewed longer -- its box (20 to 26 minutes) sits to the right of Class A's box (14 to 19), and Class B's middle value (23) is above Class A's (16). Even Class B's longest time (30) tops Class A's (24).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Two-data-set (Difficult tier) comparison. Watch for conclusions about 'how many students' -- box plots don't show counts -- or claims about individual students.

sample_items.stem: Using the two box plots: a student concludes, "Class B has more students than Class A because its box is wider." Explain why this conclusion is NOT supported.
sample_items.answer: Box width shows the SPREAD of the middle half of the times, not how many students there are. A box plot never displays the number of data points, so no conclusion about class size can come from it.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Judging someone else's reasoning -- the Above-band demand. The wider-box-means-more-data misread is the target.

vocabulary.definition: A statement about the data set that the display's numbers can back up.
A range of values one histogram bar covers, like 14-16 feet.
The count a bar's height shows -- how many data values landed in that interval.
To read what a display says about the data and explain it with evidence.
The full collection of values behind the display.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 6.DS.3 -- measures of center, spread, and overall shape of distributions.

worked_example_script.text: Project the maple tree histogram: bars 2, 5, 8, 3 over intervals 10-12, 12-14, 14-16, 16-18 feet, with the question 'How tall are the young maple trees?'
Two axes, two jobs. Touch the bottom axis -- what does it measure? Touch the side axis -- what does it count?
If the student says the side axis is 'feet' or hesitates, stop and label both axes in their own words before going on. Everything downstream depends on this.
The tallest bar reaches 8. Does that mean some tree is 8 feet tall? What is that 8 actually telling us?
The 8 counts trees -- eight trees are between 14 and 16 feet. No tree in this data is 8 feet tall; the shortest interval starts at 10.
Now let's answer the ranger's question. Where do MOST of the trees fall? Which bars would you combine, and what do they add up to?
12 to 16 feet: 5 + 8 = 13 of the 18 trees -- well over half. Notice the shape of the conclusion: interval, counts, and a 'because.'
A friend claims 'the tallest tree is 18 feet.' Is that supported, or does the histogram only pin it inside an interval?
Your turn: write one more supported conclusion about these trees, with the numbers that defend it.

practice_problems.stem: A histogram bar over the interval 10-15 rises to 6. Say in words what that bar means.
practice_problems.answer: Six data values fall between 10 and 15 -- the 6 counts values; it is not a data value itself.

practice_problems.stem: On a histogram of 12 values with bars 2, 7, 3: which interval holds the most data, and how do you know?
practice_problems.answer: The middle interval -- its bar is tallest (7 of the 12 values).

practice_problems.stem: A histogram of 25 plant heights has bars 3, 10, 9, 3 over intervals 4-6, 6-8, 8-10, 10-12 inches. Write a supported conclusion about where most plant heights fall.
practice_problems.answer: Most plants are between 6 and 10 inches: 10 + 9 = 19 of the 25 plants, over three-quarters of the data.
practice_problems.notes: Conclusion must cite intervals AND counts.

practice_problems.stem: Using that same plant histogram: a student claims 'the tallest plant is 12 inches.' Supported or not?
practice_problems.answer: Not supported -- the histogram only shows the tallest plant is somewhere between 10 and 12 inches; exact values were grouped away.
practice_problems.notes: Overreach check inside a conclusions task.

practice_problems.stem: Two box plots: Team X (min 5, box 8-14, median 11, max 18) and Team Y (min 9, box 13-17, median 15, max 20) show points scored. Which team generally scored more? Cite two features.
practice_problems.answer: Team Y -- its median (15) is above Team X's (11), and its whole box (13-17) sits to the right of Team X's (8-14).
practice_problems.notes: Two-data-set comparison, the spec's Difficult tier.

practice_problems.stem: A histogram of 16 pumpkin weights has bars 2, 4, 7, 3 over 2-4, 4-6, 6-8, 8-10 pounds. Read Rosa's conclusion, find the error, and fix it.
shown_work: Rosa: "The tallest bar reaches 7, so the biggest pumpkin weighs 7 pounds."
practice_problems.answer: Rosa read the bar HEIGHT as a weight. The 7 counts pumpkins -- seven pumpkins weigh between 6 and 8 pounds. The biggest pumpkin is actually in the last interval, somewhere between 8 and 10 pounds; the histogram can't say exactly.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: frequency read as data value, plus the exact-value overreach.

practice_problems.stem: Sketch (or describe) a histogram of 20 values where the claim 'most values are more than 50' is TRUE, using intervals 30-40, 40-50, 50-60, 60-70. Give your four bar heights.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 2, 4, 9, 5 -- because 9 + 5 = 14 of 20 values exceed 50. Any heights summing to 20 with the last two bars > 10 total work.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction: build data to support a conclusion.

practice_problems.stem: Why can a line plot support the conclusion 'exactly 3 students scored 10' but a histogram of the same scores cannot?
practice_problems.answer: A line plot keeps every individual value, so you can count dots at 10. A histogram groups scores into intervals, so a 10 disappears into its interval's count -- exact-value conclusions are no longer supported.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch tying conclusions back to what each display keeps.

activities.title: Rosa's Seven-Pound Pumpkin
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Rosa's claim that 'the biggest pumpkin weighs 7 pounds' and hunt for what the 7 really counts.
2. They label both axes in their own words: sideways = weights, up = number of pumpkins.
3. Pairs write two corrected statements: one about the 6-8 interval and one about the biggest pumpkin.
4. Debrief: which axis does a bar's HEIGHT belong to?

content.worked_problem: Histogram of 16 pumpkin weights: bars 2, 4, 7, 3 over intervals 2-4, 4-6, 6-8, 8-10 pounds. Rosa says the biggest pumpkin weighs 7 pounds because the tallest bar reaches 7.
content.error_step: Rosa read the bar height (a count of pumpkins) as a pumpkin's weight.
content.why: Bar height lives on the frequency axis -- it counts data values in the interval. Weights live on the horizontal axis. The biggest pumpkin is in the rightmost nonzero interval (8-10 lb), and its exact weight is unknowable from a histogram.

activities.title: Supported or Not Supported?
materials: One projected histogram (5K times: bars 1, 3, 9, 7 over 20-25, 25-30, 30-35, 35-40 minutes)
activities.instructions:
1. Groups sort claim cards into SUPPORTED and NOT SUPPORTED using only the projected histogram.
2. Every SUPPORTED card needs the numbers that back it; every NOT SUPPORTED card needs the reason (wrong count? exact value? data not shown?).
3. Groups write one new claim for each pile and trade with another group.
4. Debrief: what do all the unsupported claims have in common?

cards.text: Most runners took 30 minutes or longer.
The 30-35 minute interval had the most runners.
Exactly 20 runners are shown in the data.
The fastest runner finished in exactly 20 minutes.
The oldest runner was the slowest.
Nine runners finished in exactly 32 minutes.

activities.title: Two-Class Showdown
materials: Two prepared box plots on one number line (Class A vs Class B review minutes)
activities.instructions:
1. Groups study the paired box plots and write three comparison conclusions using the frame: '___ generally ___ because ___ and ___.'
2. One conclusion must be a TRAP the group writes on purpose -- something the plots do NOT support (like 'Class B has more students').
3. Groups trade papers and find each other's trap.
4. Debrief: list on the board what box plots can support (position, spread, medians) vs. cannot (counts, individuals, exact values).

strategy_links.why: Setting Rosa's height-as-value conclusion beside a correctly defended one isolates exactly where analysis goes wrong.
Draft-a-conclusion, defend-to-partner, share-out mirrors the claim-evidence structure this skill demands.
Thinking aloud through 'which bars? what do they total? out of how many?' models the evidence chain students must internalize.

questioning_prompts: What does the height of that bar count -- feet, or trees?
Say your conclusion, then point to the exact bars or box features that back it up.
Is that claim about the whole data set, or about one individual the display can't see?
More than half -- prove it. What do the qualifying bars add to, out of how many?
Could the exact largest value be read off this display? Where does it hide?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads a bar's height as a data value -- 'the tallest bar is 8, so a tree is 8 feet tall' -- or draws conclusions with no counts behind them.
misconception_redirects.say: Put one finger on the bottom axis and one on the side axis, and say what each measures. The bar's HEIGHT belongs to the side axis -- it counts data points. Now restate your conclusion citing an interval AND its count.
misconception_redirects.praise: You anchored each number to its axis and backed the conclusion with counts -- that's real data reasoning.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student draws conclusions a display can't support -- exact values from a histogram, or 'more students' from a wider box plot.
misconception_redirects.say: Before you conclude, ask: did this display keep that information? A histogram groups exact values away; a box plot never counts people. What CAN you honestly say from what's here?
misconception_redirects.praise: You stayed inside what the display actually shows -- that's an honest conclusion.

quick_checks.prompt: Histogram bars: 2, 9, 4 over intervals 0-10, 10-20, 20-30. Finish: 'Most of the data is between ___ and ___ because ___.'
quick_checks.look_for: 10 and 20, because 9 of the 15 values sit there. A student citing '9' as a data value or picking 20-30 ('bigger numbers') hasn't separated count from value.

quick_checks.prompt: Two box plots, B shifted right of A. True or false: 'B must have more data points.' Why?
quick_checks.look_for: False -- box plots show position and spread, never counts. 'True' flags the wider/righter-means-more misread.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, reading a line plot, the standard's on-grade core. If the student passes, move up to S5 (match a question to the display that answers it) and S6 (analyze histograms and box plots to defend a conclusion). If S4 fails, drop one grade to the looking-back skills: B1 checks reading a line plot and B2 checks reading a bar graph and frequency table, the two grade 5 data-display skills the standard is built on. If those wobble, the foundations locate the gap in grades 3 and 4: F1 reads a scaled bar graph and F2 counts marks on a fractional line plot. S1, S2, and S3 stay available to probe the standard's own question-writing and data-organizing steps.
